title: Kitchener 2051 growth approaches and demolition applications
subtitle: Two demolition permits, Housing for All progress update, and upcoming engagement on the new Official Plan
overview: The Planning and Strategic Initiatives Committee recommended the criteria that will guide the next round of public engagement on Kitchener 2051, the project to write the city's new Official Plan. The community parameters and technical evaluation criteria will be used to talk with residents about how and where the city could grow {{vote:m3}}. Engagement includes an event on April 5, community conversation kits through April, and ongoing talks with First Nations and the Community Working Group.

The committee also recommended approving two demolition control applications, for 153 Courtland Avenue East {{vote:m1}} and 101 Clive Road {{vote:m2}}. The Courtland Avenue East house is a heritage-designated property that was allowed to decay. The city is the applicant in that case, as a last resort under property standards rules.

The committee also received the Housing for All update for information, and councillors asked staff about how some actions were labelled as achieved. A planning application for 288-292 Lawrence Avenue was on the agenda but not considered. Staff expect it to return at a future meeting with new notice. These recommendations go to Council for a final decision.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended that the community parameters and technical evaluation criteria be used to inform continued community and collaborator engagement on approaches to growth.
The committee recommended approving demolition of a single detached dwelling at 153 Courtland Avenue East, as set out in staff report DSD-2025-092.
The committee recommended approving demolition of a two-storey single detached dwelling at 101 Clive Road, as set out in staff report DSD-2025-107.

debate: On the Courtland Avenue East demolition, a councillor asked how the city can prevent heritage buildings from decaying to the point of demolition. Staff said the property is designated under the Ontario Heritage Act, and an independent engineer's assessment found repair would cost far more than demolition. They said they have since inspected all vacant heritage-designated properties and issued property standards orders where needed.

Staff explained that the demolition control application only decides whether a dwelling can be removed without an immediate replacement. The property keeps its residential zoning, so the owner or a later purchaser could redevelop it.

On Kitchener 2051, councillors asked about reaching groups not yet listed, including the accessibility and environmental advisory committees, condo and high-rise residents, and students through the My Ideal Kitchener program. Staff welcomed these suggestions. They said most central neighbourhood secondary plans were repealed last year, leaving the Dundee Secondary Plan as the active one.

On the Housing for All update, a councillor questioned whether items marked achieved, such as treating people with housing need as experts and tracking rental evictions, were really complete. Staff agreed the work is ongoing. They said a report on evictions due to renovations is expected in June.

A councillor also asked what addressing NIMBYism means in the plan. Staff said it is about constructive dialogue and helping residents understand the development process. They said it does not mean ruling out opposition to a development.
